fun_highlights: The callback system is the game's single strongest mechanic: a choice at age 6 (keeping a stray, looking away from the lonely child) surfaces again at 48 as a concrete moral reckoning (cb_lookaway, cb_outcast_return). This is the genre's best loop — Alter Ego gestured at it, A Life delivers it with real prose weight.

Vocation gates are structurally sound. A soldier life draws a different card cluster than a scholar or maker life: a_soldier_service -> m_soldier_ghost -> e_soldier_old vs a_scholar_question -> m_scholar_legacy -> e_scholar_old. The transcripts confirm this works: Vesna Vane reads differently from Tariq Salvedi.

Era collisions are the freshest thing in the design. The vocation x era intersection cards (vx_scholar_turning, vx_soldier_war, vx_maker_plenty) produce genuinely novel situations. Tobias Vane born into a plague era gets w_plague_tend; the same person in a settled era would never see it. This is the kind of mechanical collision the genre rarely achieves.

The dynasty layer — seat, repute, motto, heirlooms, secret — is more designed than BitLife's vague 'legacy' or Alter Ego's absent one. The book-too-hard-to-read passing from Niall to Saoirse to Ingrid across Dynasty 10, with each generation choosing differently how to use it, is a minor emergent triumph.

The 'competing goods' cards (x_honest_or_kind, x_loyalty_truth, x_dream_or_duty) are rare genre departures from the binary virtue/vice framing. Neither answer is plainly right, and the prose makes that felt rather than announced.

Solitary and childless life-shapes (m_solitary, a_chosen_family, e_solitary, e_childless) are properly content-bearing, not just dead-ends. The transcripts show them appearing and reading as complete arcs.
staleness: The wanderer vocation monoculture is severe and visible in the transcripts. Across 18 lives examined in depth, the wanderer calling (or its functional twin, the 'road') appears in roughly half of all founders and a majority of subsequent heirs: Junia Holloway, Hale Bjornsen, Anders Vasquez, Caleb Quint, Tamsin Aldecott, Annika Voss, Pavel Salvedi, Otto Vane. The wanderer arc's mid-life card (m_wanderer_return) consequently fires constantly — 'Went home at last, and found it had gone on without him' — becoming the most-seen single-life log line in the sample. The weighting or draw-nudge for the road vocation appears systematically too high relative to scholar and maker.

The late-love/late-marriage monoculture has been partially fixed by the engine (the brief comment in drawCard() acknowledges it), but the transcripts reveal it persists structurally. In Dynasties 3-13, the majority of long-lived characters still marry past age 50 or at minimum past 40. The opening line 'Married X late, and found the lateness made the vow weigh more, not less' appears in Dynasty 4 (Anders, age 57), Dynasty 5 (Liv, age 57), Dynasty 7 (Cassian, age 41), Dynasty 9 (Caleb, age 50), Dynasty 11 (Tariq, age 55), Dynasty 13 (Cassian, age 58), Dynasty 13 (Cosima, age 55). The fix addressed the symptom in the engine but the pool of 'late' marriage lines is still being served into almost every life.

A recurring structural beat — love appears late, child arrives even later, wanderer eventually returns home, elder counts the doors closed — is not just a single-life template but a multi-dynasty template shared across the majority of runs. By Dynasty 8-10 an experienced reader can anticipate the emotional arc of a given life before half its cards are drawn.

Several high-weight cards produce near-identical log lines across dynasties. 'Counted, at the end of the road, the doors he had closed in order to keep walking' appears in Dynasties 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11 — seven times in thirteen dynasties, making it the game's closest thing to an obligatory late-life sentence. Similarly 'Said he hoped to be remembered as kind' with the 'That I was kind' choice fires in Dynasties 4, 7, 9 across consecutive generations. The anti-repetition guard (RECENT_LINES in epitaphFor) works for epitaphs but has no equivalent for log lines generated by choice do() functions.

The choices themselves are almost always binary, and both poles are identifiable archetypes: open/closed, give/keep, stay/go, tend/ignore. Reigns and Cultist Simulator earn freshness from choices whose outcomes are opaque or mechanically surprising. A Life's choices are almost always emotionally legible at the point of selection, which reduces replaying for discovery — you know what kind of person each button creates before you click it.

The dynasty meta-layer offers less real steering than it implies. The seat/repute/motto system is largely an accounting consequence of individual choices, not a target you actively build toward in ways that meaningfully constrain individual lives. A player wanting to build a scholarly house cannot gate specific scholarly opportunities to that house mid-play; they can only hope the right cards appear. The contrast with Reigns — where each answer has a visible mechanical cost you're managing — is sharp.

improvements.what: Rebalance vocation draw weights: reduce the road/wanderer nudge by at least 40% and increase maker and scholar nudges proportionally. Add a per-dynasty cap: if two consecutive lives chose wanderer, suppress the draw-nudge for a third.
improvements.why: The transcripts show wanderer is effectively the default vocation. The structural variety the vocation system promises — four genuinely different adult arcs — collapses when one path is taken by 50%+ of lives. Scholar and maker each have richer card clusters (masterwork, shop, legacy) that go unplayed for multiple dynasties at a stretch.

improvements.what: Add a per-session log-line deduplication guard equivalent to the RECENT_LINES epitaph guard, covering the 8-10 highest-frequency do() outputs. The 'counted, at the end of the road, the doors closed' line and the 'said he hoped to be remembered as kind' line are the worst offenders; flag any line that has fired more than 3 times in the current session and suppress it in favor of the next variant.
improvements.why: The juror's single strongest staleness signal in the genre is verbatim repetition of emotional lines across consecutive lives. The game has excellent line variety within each card's pool; the problem is that the same card fires too often, burning through one variant and looping to the next until patterns are visible.

improvements.what: Add 2-3 true hard-gate dynasty events that only a house with a specific reputation AND a specific era can access, and make them meaningfully alter what choices are available in that life, not just which log line is written. Example: a scholarly house in a turning era gets a card where the family's accumulated learning is suddenly socially weaponizable — with real consequences for the seat if they refuse.
improvements.why: The vocation x era intersections (vx_*) are the freshest content in the game because they produce genuinely unexpected situations. The dynasty-reputation layer should do the same: a tainted house in a plague era, a ruthless house in plenty years. Right now repute-gated cards (r_scholar_door, r_hard_name) gate content but the outcomes are still purely individual-life stat adjustments.

improvements.what: Break the binary choice grammar in at least 8-10 more cards across the adult and midlife stages. Add a third option that is not a middle-of-the-road compromise but a structurally different response — a deflection, a delay, an unexpected action. Use the competing-goods cards (x_honest_or_kind, x_loyalty_truth) as the template.
improvements.why: Binary choices produce legible people quickly but exhaust their novelty faster. The genre's most replayable entries (Cultist Simulator's resource-burn decisions, Reigns' lateral consequences) gain longevity from choices whose second-order effects are opaque. A Life's choices feel honest but predictable — by dynasty 5 the player models each character before the choice resolves.

improvements.what: Cap the late-marriage line variants more aggressively: force the engine to prefer the 'young marriage' variants when P.age < 35 at marry-time, and only serve 'lateness made the vow weigh more' variants when the character is genuinely old (45+). Currently the 'late' framing fires at ages as young as 38-41, making the emotional register feel unearned.
improvements.why: The late-marriage language is affecting and the variants are well-written, but they're being served into situations where the 'lateness' isn't narratively true — the character is in their late 30s, which the prose treats as old. This flattens the emotional register and makes mid-30s marriages read the same as 55-year-old ones.

verdict: A Life is a technically accomplished, compassionately written life-sim with two genuine innovations — the callback arc system and the vocation x era collision cards — but it goes stale around dynasty 6-8 because one vocation dominates by weight, a handful of late-life log lines repeat across almost every run, and the binary choice grammar limits how much discovery survives a second or third dynasty.
